English translation

Giorgia Capra

Persephone, queen of the Catanaeans

commentary

The text is lost, but recorded by Gualtherus as being on the base of a clay statue one cubit high. There is much debate in the scholarship post-Gualtherus over whether the text and statue was a forgery or genuine. Kaibel and Franz both note that the existence of such a statue, and the accompanying text, at such an early date (pre-1624) is against the idea of a forgery. On the text of line 3, Gualtherus' presentation, is entirely compatible with the proposed reading of Franz and others, of a damaged final line (a gap for the iota, the lambda-like trace being the upper part of a rhomboid omega, and a lacuna following).

Βασιλίς is a cultic epithet of Aphrodite (cf. Hesych. 284 Latte s.v. βασιλίνδα), whose cult in the form of Ἀφροδίτη Βασιλίς is attested above all at Tarentum (SEG 40.898), perhaps imported from Sparta (cf. SEG 49.412). The epithet is, however, also applied to other divine entities (such as the deified Roma: IGUR III 1262, l. 4), whereas the form βασιλίσσα, supplemented by Kaibel (ap. IG XIV 450), who assumes a lacuna to the right, is more common and is used primarily for historical queens. By contrast, Manganaro (1988, 68 n. 346) suggests that the statue was dedicated to Persephone (reading a dative in l. 1) by a woman named Βασιλίς; for the name, attested in another fourth-century AD inscription from Catania, see IMusCatania 212 (= ISic000647). L. 3 seems to refer to the ethnic: Persephone would thus be queen of the inhabitants of Catania. It is also possible that the genitive referred to the entire Catanian people, who would have been responsible for the dedication, as in I.Akrai 65. Manganaro (1988, 68 n. 346), however, read κατ’ ὄναρ, hypothesizing a dedication carried out following a dream; another imperial-period parallel from Catania is attested in BE 1962.388 (= ISic003004). On the cult for Demeter and Persephones in Catania, see Amata 2016. The only basis for dating would be the limited evidence for letterforms, with rhomboid letters attested on the island from later C2 BCE onwards.
